sections.markdown:
## C2 — Confusable pairs and continuation facts: headlight aim, night parking, wipers and defroster, rain habits, fog conduct, hidden ice, hot-day rain, skid recovery, rumble stripes, flood depth, wind, sun glare, getting unstuck, snow and ice errors and hail
Confusable pairs and continuation facts; each block ties to one manual page, and any hint metadata sits only in the trailing line of a block.

FACT_ID: sec11-R01 | anchor: A01
Headlight power fades sharply with distance, which is why the lights must be in good working order to meet the legal seeing distance. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0088]

FACT_ID: sec11-R02 | anchor: A01
Check your owner's manual for how to aim your headlights, or have a mechanic at a reputable garage or dealership align them. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0088]

FACT_ID: sec11-R03 | anchor: A02
A parked car's lit headlights are a bigger hazard when the car sits on the wrong side of the road. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0089]

FACT_ID: sec11-R04 | anchor: A02
Parking on an interstate shoulder is banned except in an emergency, and you may not park on any paved or unpaved part of an entrance or exit ramp unless the vehicle is disabled. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0089]

FACT_ID: sec11-R05 | anchor: A02
Keep your wiper blades in good shape, and wait a few seconds after rain begins before turning them on so there is enough water to clear the glass rather than smear grime. [A02]
Why it matters: group wipers; difficulty low.
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0089]

FACT_ID: sec11-R06 | anchor: A02
Use the defroster or the air conditioner to keep your windows and mirrors clear in bad weather. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0089]

FACT_ID: sec11-R07 | anchor: A02
Rain calls for signaling turns and lane changes early and braking well ahead of a stop so drivers behind know what you plan. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0089]

FACT_ID: sec11-R08 | anchor: A02
In fog or smoke, keep the radio off or low and do not use a cell phone, so you can hear the traffic around you. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0089]

FACT_ID: sec11-R09 | anchor: A02
In fog, be patient, keep to the right, avoid passing, avoid crossing traffic unless you must, and do not stop on the roadway unless it is truly necessary. [A02]
Why it matters: group fog; confusable stopping on the road versus pulling fully off.
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0089]

FACT_ID: sec11-R10 | anchor: A02
If your car stalls or breaks down in fog or smoke, move away from it to avoid being hurt. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0089]

FACT_ID: sec11-R11 | anchor: A02
In fog, consider putting off your trip until it clears, and obey the warning devices set up in fog-prone areas. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0089]

FACT_ID: sec11-R12 | anchor: A02
On cold, wet days, spots shaded by trees or buildings can hide ice, because they freeze first and dry out last. [A02]
Why it matters: group hidden ice; confusable shaded spots versus bridges.
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0089]

FACT_ID: sec11-R13 | anchor: A02
Bridges and overpasses can hide ice because they tend to freeze before the rest of the road. [A02]
Why it matters: group hidden ice; confusable bridges versus shaded spots.
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0089]

FACT_ID: sec11-R14 | anchor: A02
When rain starts on a hot day, heat-raised oil in the asphalt makes the pavement extremely slippery for the first few minutes, until the rain washes it away. [A02]
Why it matters: group slippery roads; confusable hot-day rain versus first rain film.
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0089]

FACT_ID: sec11-R15 | anchor: A03
Close to the freezing point, an icy road can be more slippery than it is at colder temperatures. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0090]

FACT_ID: sec11-R16 | anchor: A03
Once a skidding car begins to straighten, turn the wheel back the other way, or the car may swing around and start a new skid in the opposite direction. [A03]
Why it matters: group skids; difficulty medium.
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0090]

FACT_ID: sec11-R17 | anchor: A03
Keep making small left and right steering corrections after a skid until the vehicle is moving down the road under your control again. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0090]

FACT_ID: sec11-R18 | anchor: A03
The best defense against skids is to avoid them by watching the weather and slowing down well before your stopping point. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0090]

FACT_ID: sec11-R19 | anchor: A03
Rumble stripes are edge lines painted over a row of indentations; their main job is to make the edge line easier to see on wet nights, while the vibration and noise are a side effect. [A03]
Why it matters: group pavement markings; confusable main purpose versus side effect.
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0090]

FACT_ID: sec11-R20 | anchor: A03
A heavy vehicle is no protection in a flood, because cars float through buoyancy and trucks or SUVs gain only six to twelve more inches of clearance. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0090]

FACT_ID: sec11-R21 | anchor: A03
Once swept downstream, a car often rolls or flips and the driver has only a few seconds to get out, and many panicked drivers are later found still belted in. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0090]

FACT_ID: sec11-R22 | anchor: A04
As little as six to twelve inches of water can cost you control of the car, while about two feet is enough to float most cars downstream. [A04]
Why it matters: group flood depth; confusable losing control versus being carried away.
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0091]

FACT_ID: sec11-R23 | anchor: A04
Never drive through floodwater or across a flowing stream, and if your vehicle stalls in water, leave it right away and head for higher ground. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0091]

FACT_ID: sec11-R24 | anchor: A04
Watch for flooding at highway dips, low spots and around bridges, do not camp or park beside streams when storms threaten, and take special care at night when flood dangers are harder to see. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0091]

FACT_ID: sec11-R25 | anchor: A04
During severe thunderstorms, listen to your car radio and stay alert. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0091]

FACT_ID: sec11-R26 | anchor: A04
Strong crosswinds make a vehicle harder to control, especially a camper, a large recreational vehicle, a car towing a trailer or a lightweight vehicle, so slow down. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0091]

FACT_ID: sec11-R27 | anchor: A04
Watch for crosswinds that can push you toward the side or middle of the road when you come out of a sheltered stretch into open space. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0091]

FACT_ID: sec11-R28 | anchor: A04
When towing a trailer, wind from a passing truck or bus can make your rig jackknife, so accelerate slowly once it passes to keep the trailer tracking straight. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0091]

FACT_ID: sec11-R29 | anchor: A04
A headwind may require more gas and makes steering harder, while a tailwind raises your speed, so you must slow and begin braking sooner. [A04]
Why it matters: group wind; confusable headwind versus tailwind.
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0091]

FACT_ID: sec11-R30 | anchor: A04
Driving toward the sun in early morning or late afternoon creates glare, which sunglasses, clean windows and sun visors reduce. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0091]

FACT_ID: sec11-R31 | anchor: A04
When the sun is behind you, oncoming drivers face the glare and may not see your turn signals or even your car. [A04]
Why it matters: group sun glare; confusable sun ahead versus sun behind.
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0091]

FACT_ID: sec11-R32 | anchor: A04
To free a car stuck in mud or snow, shift to low gear with the front wheels straight, press the gas gently without spinning the wheels, and drive forward as far as you can. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0091]

FACT_ID: sec11-R33 | anchor: A04
Then shift to reverse and back up slowly as far as possible, and repeat this forward and backward rocking until the car rolls free. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0091]

FACT_ID: sec11-R34 | anchor: A04
In deep mud or snow you can put boards or branches under the tires, but never while the wheels are spinning or the vehicle is in gear. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0091]

FACT_ID: sec11-R35 | anchor: A04
Carrying tire chains year-round can keep you from getting stuck; pull far to the right before fitting them, and put them on before driving into snow or mud. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0091]

FACT_ID: sec11-R36 | anchor: A04
Most drivers' three big errors on snow and ice are overpowering and spinning the wheels, over-braking and sliding them, and over-steering into a skid. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0091]

FACT_ID: sec11-R37 | anchor: A04
Before driving in winter, clear snow, ice and frost from every window, and carry a quality ice scraper with a brush for windows, lights and outside mirrors. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0091]

FACT_ID: sec11-R38 | anchor: A05
Use your headlights whenever weather limits visibility, so other drivers can see you. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0092]

FACT_ID: sec11-R39 | anchor: A05
On ice or snow, start slowly and avoid spinning the wheels, and keep your speed steady and slow but not too slow. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0092]

FACT_ID: sec11-R40 | anchor: A05
In deeper snow you often need the car's momentum to keep moving, and good front tire treads or snow tires improve steering. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0092]

FACT_ID: sec11-R41 | anchor: A05
On a low-traction surface at 20 mph, your stopping distance can stretch to 200 feet or more. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0092]

FACT_ID: sec11-R42 | anchor: A05
The sunny side of a hill may be merely wet while the shady side is covered with thin ice. [A05]
Why it matters: group hidden ice; confusable sunny side versus shady side.
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0092]

FACT_ID: sec11-R43 | anchor: A05
Ice usually forms on bridges before the roads leading up to them, and a long ice patch behind a car that stopped ahead of you can make you skid into it. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0092]

FACT_ID: sec11-R44 | anchor: A05
Where stop-and-go traffic packs fresh snow hard, it soon becomes extremely slippery, and steering to one side of the packed track can help you avoid the slickest part. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0092]

FACT_ID: sec11-R45 | anchor: A05
In a hailstorm or sleet, the manual says to seek shelter by driving under an overpass or bridge. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0092]
